editorial.titleTr: [Editorial] Broken Personnel System, "Personnel Decisions Are Kim Hyun-ji" Surfaces Again
summaryTr: Controversy reignites over vetting of justice and gender equality ministers
Allegations of president's close aides' private interference in Blue House personnel system
Call for rigorous investigation by special inspector as public system collapses
editorial.bodyTr: The controversy surrounding the confirmation hearings for the Justice Ministry and Gender Equality and Family Ministry nominees and allegations of private intervention in the presidential office's personnel system highlight a troubling erosion of public institutions. As reports suggest close associates of the president may have interfered in personnel decisions, we call for a rigorous and impartial investigation by the special inspector general. The integrity of our administrative systems depends on ensuring that appointments are made through transparent and merit-based processes, free from factional influence or behind-the-scenes maneuvering. Without swift action to restore confidence in these procedures, the public's trust in government institutions will continue to deteriorate.

editorials.titleTr: Editorial: A Year After the Sept. 7 Plan, Seoul Apartment Prices Rise for 82 Consecutive Weeks
summaryTr: One year after the Sept. 7 real estate measures, Seoul apartment prices rise for 82 consecutive weeks.
Market instability persists due to supply shortage and regulation-focused policies.
Negative assessment of government real estate policy ranks first in economic livelihood sector.
editorials.bodyTr: An analysis of the Lee Jae-myung administration's real estate measures announced on September 7, one year into their implementation, reveals persistent market instability. Seoul apartment prices have risen for 82 consecutive weeks due to insufficient supply and policy focused primarily on regulation. As policy credibility declines and moral controversies surround the nominees for minister of land, infrastructure and transport and minister of economy and finance, negative assessments of the government's real estate policies rank first among economic and livelihood-related issues.

editorial.titleTr: [Editorial] Kim Seung-won Allegations Keep Mounting—Is He Fit for Public Office?
summaryTr: Justice Minister nominee Kim Seung-won delivered a petition to the Food and Drug Administration through a broker.
The head of the Food and Drug Administration instructed staff to accept the petition, undermining the public interest.
Financial transactions, family favoritism, and past inflammatory remarks compound doubts about his fitness for public office.
editorial.bodyTr: Suspicions surrounding Kim Seung-won, the nominee for justice minister, continue to mount by the day. According to a recording released by independent lawmaker Han Dong-hun, Kim received a request from broker Yang to help expedite clinical trial approval for a COVID-19 new drug, and his intervention on behalf of the broker went so far as to pressure a senior official at the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety. When Kim asked which department handled the matter, Yang replied that it would "not go beyond the division chief level." The ministry's secretary to the commissioner then texted the relevant division chief: "Assemblyman Kim sent a text message. Please make sure such matters don't come up from that side anymore." A lawmaker took the initiative in seeking favors, and the food and drug safety commissioner essentially instructed his staff to accommodate the request. It is enough to provoke public anger that public officials who should represent the common good acted as brokers for private interests. Kim's mention of "tens of billions of won" at the moment of food and drug safety approval during his conversation with Yang further fuels suspicion. According to the recording, Yang brought up delays in the clinical approval of Genencel's new drug treatment, saying "300 billion won in investment has already been secured." Kim then responded that once the food and drug safety approval came through, "it would be possible to earn tens of billions of won," and asked Yang to send materials by email. Yang also mentioned that it would be "good timing for your brother's election next year," referring to the presidential election, and said he "tried to give Cash 2000 to Seung-won oppa." This is why initial suspicions arose that financial dealings or private interests were involved. The private conversation between Kim and Yang, in which they exchanged sentiments like "I'm getting teary-eyed wanting to see you," also raises eyebrows among the public. Regarding suspicions that Kim's spouse, as director of a social cooperative, had their eldest son and second daughter receive salaries through a "salary splitting" scheme, it must also be determined whether there is legal liability. The public well remembers that Kim previously used crude language, "GSGG," toward the National Assembly speaker during the media arbitration law initiative, and when controversy ensued, he offered a specious explanation. It also needs to be clarified why the prosecution, which initially indicted Kim on bribery charges and sought an eight-month prison sentence, ultimately granted him a suspended prosecution. The justice minister is a symbolic position representing fair law enforcement. The mere mention of someone plagued by allegations of quid pro quo lobbying, abuse of private authority, and family-related improprieties for a post that demands above all else rigorous moral standards and integrity is itself an affront to the civil service. The public questions whether Kim qualifies to serve not only as justice minister, but in any public office whatsoever.

editorial.title: Hormuz dilemma
editorial.body: Seoul must seek ways to help maritime security without being drawn into Middle East conflict A maritime bottleneck carrying most of South Korea’s energy imports is a perilous arena for symbolic alliance gestures. Yet Seoul faces mounting pressure to deploy forces to the Strait of Hormuz, where deepening conflict threatens vital commercial shipping. The presidential office said Friday that no decision had been made and that various options remained under review. Any contribution, it said, would have to preserve the nation’s defense readiness on the Korean Peninsula and comply with domestic law. Those are sensible guardrails. They should remain the starting point, not boxes to be checked before a decision has already been made. The strategic dilemma is real. About 70 percent of Korea’s crude oil imports pass through the strait, making freedom of navigation directly relevant to its economic security. The country also has a legitimate interest in helping keep an international sea lane open. It cannot reasonably expect others to protect routes on which its energy-dependent economy relies. The question is how to contribute without making Korean personnel part of a widening war. The alliance, meanwhile, cannot be ignored. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly complained that Korea has declined to make a sufficient contribution to the effort around Iran. Washington has been pressing Seoul across security, trade and investment issues, while talks between the allies have encountered renewed difficulties. The temptation to treat the Strait of Hormuz as merely another bargaining chip is understandable, if shortsighted. That would be a costly way to manage an alliance. A military alliance should not become an accounting ledger in which a contribution to one conflict is exchanged for concessions elsewhere. Decisions involving Korean service members and the use of military force require their own standards. Linking a deployment to semiconductor negotiations, tariffs or other bilateral disputes would weaken the nation’s position precisely when its leaders need room for independent judgment. Nor should the label “noncombat” create a false sense of security. A maritime patrol aircraft gathering information or a support vessel supplying military forces may have a defensive purpose, yet such assets operate within the machinery of war. In an active conflict zone, they can become targets regardless of their formal mission. A single attack could expose Korea to retaliation and create pressure for a deeper military response. The constitutional issue is equally important. Article 60 requires National Assembly consent for the overseas deployment of the armed forces. The requirement is not a procedural nuisance. It exists because sending military personnel abroad carries consequences that cannot be reversed as easily as a diplomatic statement. If Seoul proceeds, the mission, command structure, rules of engagement, duration and conditions for withdrawal should be clearly defined before lawmakers are asked to approve it. There is also Tehran. Korea has maintained pragmatic relations with Iran for decades, and worsening those ties could complicate the very energy security that a Hormuz deployment is meant to protect. Military involvement carries a paradox: An effort to secure shipping could expose Korean vessels and Koreans themselves to greater danger. There are alternatives. Japan’s case illustrates that an ally can contribute to maritime security while maintaining legal and operational boundaries. Seoul could work with European partners on freedom of navigation while restricting any military involvement to strictly defensive or postconflict roles, such as mine clearance and humanitarian assistance. The choice is not between satisfying Washington and jeopardizing the alliance; it is between contributing on terms the country can defend and accepting a deployment whose logic could widen as the war escalates. The government must state its legal constraints and defense priorities clearly to Washington. Hormuz calls for a contribution grounded in national interests, not a loyalty test measured by how far Seoul is willing to follow Washington into danger. editorial.bodyTr:
서울은 중동 분쟁에 휘말리지 않으면서 해양 안보를 돕는 방안을 모색해야 한다

한국의 에너지 수입 대부분을 운반하는 해상 병목 지역은 상징적 동맹 제스처를 펼치기에 위험한 장소다. 그럼에도 불구하고 서울은 호르무즈 해협에 병력을 배치하라는 압박이 증가하고 있으며, 이곳에서 심화되는 분쟁이 중요한 상업 해운을 위협하고 있다. 대통령실은 금요일 아직 결정을 내리지 않았으며 다양한 옵션을 검토 중이라고 밝혔다. 어떤 기여든 한반도 방위태세를 유지하고 국내법을 준수해야 한다고 덧붙였다. 이는 합리적인 기준이다. 이러한 기준은 출발점으로 남아 있어야 하며, 이미 결정이 내려진 후 체크해야 할 항목이 되어서는 안 된다.

전략적 딜레마는 실제로 존재한다. 한국의 원유 수입량 약 70퍼센트가 이 해협을 통과하므로 항행의 자유가 경제 안보와 직결된다. 또한 국가는 국제 해상로를 계속 열어두는 데 도움을 주는 것에 정당한 이해관계가 있다. 자국의 에너지 의존적 경제가 의존하는 해로를 타국이 보호해주기를 합리적으로 기대할 수는 없다. 문제는 한국 인력이 확대되는 전쟁의 일부가 되지 않으면서 어떻게 기여할 것인가이다.

한편 동맹관계는 무시할 수 없다. 도널드 트럼프 미국 대통령은 한국이 이란 주변 노력에 충분히 기여하지 않았다고 반복적으로 불평해 왔다. 워싱턴은 안보, 통상, 투자 문제에서 서울에 압박을 가해 왔으며, 동맹 간 회담은 새로운 어려움을 겪고 있다. 호르무즈 해협을 단순히 또 다른 협상 카드로 취급하려는 유혹은 이해할 수 있지만 근시안적이다. 이는 동맹을 관리하는 비용이 많이 드는 방식이 될 것이다. 군사 동맹이 한 분쟁에 대한 기여를 다른 곳의 양보와 맞바꾸는 회계 장부가 되어서는 안 된다. 한국 군인과 군사력 사용이 관련된 결정은 자체적인 기준이 필요하다. 배치를 반도체 협상, 관세 또는 기타 양자 분쟁과 연결하면 지도자들이 독립적인 판단의 여지를 필요로 할 정확히 그때 국가의 입지를 약화시킬 것이다.

또한 "비전투"라는 명칭이 거짓의 안전감을 만들어서는 안 된다. 정보를 수집하는 해상 순찰 항공기나 군대에 보급품을 제공하는 지원함은 방어적 목적을 가지고 있을 수 있지만, 이러한 자산은 전쟁의 기계 내에서 작동한다. 활발한 분쟁 지역에서 공식적인 임무와 무관하게 공격의 대상이 될 수 있다. 단 한 번의 공격도 한국을 보복에 노출시킬 수 있으며 더 깊은 군사 대응의 압박을 만들 수 있다.

헌법 문제는 똑같이 중요하다. 제60조는 국방력의 해외 배치에 대해 국회 동의를 요구한다. 이 요구는 절차적 번거로움이 아니다. 군인을 해외로 보내는 것이 외교 성명처럼 쉽게 되돌릴 수 없는 결과를 가져오기 때문에 존재한다. 서울이 진행한다면 임무, 지휘 구조, 교전 규칙, 기간 및 철수 조건을 의원들에게 승인을 요청하기 전에 명확히 정의해야 한다.

또한 테헤란이 있다. 한국은 수십 년간 이란과 실용적인 관계를 유지해 왔으며, 이 관계를 악화시키면 호르무즈 배치가 보호하려는 바로 그 에너지 안보를 복잡하게 만들 수 있다. 군사 관여는 역설을 가진다. 해운을 확보하려는 노력이 한국 선박과 한국인 자신을 더 큰 위험에 노출시킬 수 있다.

대안도 있다. 일본의 사례는 동맹국이 법적, 운영적 경계를 유지하면서 해양 안보에 기여할 수 있음을 보여준다. 서울은 항행의 자유에 대해 유럽 파트너와 협력하면서 군사 관여를 지뢰 제거 및 인도적 지원과 같은 엄격히 방어적 또는 전후 역할로 제한할 수 있다. 선택은 워싱턴을 만족시키거나 동맹을 위험에 빠뜨리는 것 사이가 아니다. 국가가 방어할 수 있는 조건에서 기여하거나 전쟁이 확대됨에 따라 논리가 확장될 수 있는 배치를 수용하는 것이다. 정부는 법적 제약과 방위 우선순위를 명확하게 워싱턴에 전달해야 한다. 호르무즈는 국가 이익에 기초한 기여를 요구하지, 서울이 워싱턴을 따라 위험으로 나아갈 의지로 측정하는 충성도 시험이 아니다.

editorials.title: Hormuz dilemma
editorials.body: Seoul must seek ways to help maritime security without being drawn into Middle East conflict A maritime bottleneck carrying most of South Korea’s energy imports is a perilous arena for symbolic alliance gestures. Yet Seoul faces mounting pressure to deploy forces to the Strait of Hormuz, where deepening conflict threatens vital commercial shipping. The presidential office said Friday that no decision had been made and that various options remained under review. Any contribution, it said, would have to preserve the nation’s defense readiness on the Korean Peninsula and comply with domestic law. Those are sensible guardrails. They should remain the starting point, not boxes to be checked before a decision has already been made. The strategic dilemma is real. About 70 percent of Korea’s crude oil imports pass through the strait, making freedom of navigation directly relevant to its economic security. The country also has a legitimate interest in helping keep an international sea lane open. It cannot reasonably expect others to protect routes on which its energy-dependent economy relies. The question is how to contribute without making Korean personnel part of a widening war. The alliance, meanwhile, cannot be ignored. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly complained that Korea has declined to make a sufficient contribution to the effort around Iran. Washington has been pressing Seoul across security, trade and investment issues, while talks between the allies have encountered renewed difficulties. The temptation to treat the Strait of Hormuz as merely another bargaining chip is understandable, if shortsighted. That would be a costly way to manage an alliance. A military alliance should not become an accounting ledger in which a contribution to one conflict is exchanged for concessions elsewhere. Decisions involving Korean service members and the use of military force require their own standards. Linking a deployment to semiconductor negotiations, tariffs or other bilateral disputes would weaken the nation’s position precisely when its leaders need room for independent judgment. Nor should the label “noncombat” create a false sense of security. A maritime patrol aircraft gathering information or a support vessel supplying military forces may have a defensive purpose, yet such assets operate within the machinery of war. In an active conflict zone, they can become targets regardless of their formal mission. A single attack could expose Korea to retaliation and create pressure for a deeper military response. The constitutional issue is equally important. Article 60 requires National Assembly consent for the overseas deployment of the armed forces. The requirement is not a procedural nuisance. It exists because sending military personnel abroad carries consequences that cannot be reversed as easily as a diplomatic statement. If Seoul proceeds, the mission, command structure, rules of engagement, duration and conditions for withdrawal should be clearly defined before lawmakers are asked to approve it. There is also Tehran. Korea has maintained pragmatic relations with Iran for decades, and worsening those ties could complicate the very energy security that a Hormuz deployment is meant to protect. Military involvement carries a paradox: An effort to secure shipping could expose Korean vessels and Koreans themselves to greater danger. There are alternatives. Japan’s case illustrates that an ally can contribute to maritime security while maintaining legal and operational boundaries. Seoul could work with European partners on freedom of navigation while restricting any military involvement to strictly defensive or postconflict roles, such as mine clearance and humanitarian assistance. The choice is not between satisfying Washington and jeopardizing the alliance; it is between contributing on terms the country can defend and accepting a deployment whose logic could widen as the war escalates. The government must state its legal constraints and defense priorities clearly to Washington. Hormuz calls for a contribution grounded in national interests, not a loyalty test measured by how far Seoul is willing to follow Washington into danger. The exposed data includes not only birthdates and mobile phone numbers, but also connected information (CI), which is critical for identity verification. editorials.pullQuote: 수출 1조 달러 시대를 맞이하면서 경제 성장의 과실을 국민이 체감할 수 있도록 하는 것이 중요하다.
summary: 한국 수출이 1조 달러 시대를 앞두고 있다.
경제 지표는 좋으나 국민이 체감하는 경기는 여전히 부진하다.
체감경기와 경제 성장의 괴리를 줄이는 것이 핵심 과제다.
editorials.stance: 거시경제 호조에도 불구하고 가계 피해감을 해소하기 위한 정책 개선이 필요하다는 입장
editorials.titleTr: Opinion: Export boom hits $1 trillion milestone, but closing the gap with consumer sentiment remains key challenge
summaryTr: South Korea's exports are poised to enter the trillion-dollar era.
Economic indicators are positive, but consumers still feel the economy is sluggish.
Narrowing the gap between perceived and actual economic growth is the key challenge.

leanScore.label: Center
leanScore.rationale: 거시경제 지표와 국민 체감의 괴리를 객관적으로 지적하며, 특정 계층·정책·진영을 비판하지 않고 균형잡힌 정책 개선을 제안하는 중도적 입장
